paragraphs: A classifier’s confidence should help users judge how much to trust its predictions. Calibration methods adjust that confidence, but methods that work well on familiar test data can become unreliable when the data distribution changes. This paper introduces Density-Aware Calibration, or DAC, to improve uncertainty estimates across those different conditions while preserving prediction accuracy.

DAC uses nearest-neighbor information and the classifier’s hidden representations as sources of information about uncertainty. Its central move is to look inside the network for information useful to calibration, rather than relying only on the information used by existing post-processing methods. The authors also examine the importance of hidden layers and make DAC compatible with existing calibration approaches.

Experiments report consistently improved calibration across multiple architectures, datasets, and evaluation measures. The improvements extend to shifted and out-of-domain data while retaining strong calibration on familiar data. The authors also report substantial improvements for large networks pretrained on extensive datasets. These findings support hidden representations as a useful resource for making confidence estimates more robust under the evaluated distribution changes.
icml-2023-beyond-in-domain-scenarios-rob.tldr: DAC uses nearest-neighbor information from hidden representations to improve calibration under distribution shifts while preserving accuracy.

paragraphs: In partially observable reinforcement learning, an agent receives observations without directly seeing the underlying state. Large or continuous state and observation spaces make this especially difficult. This paper identifies a structured setting in which an algorithm can find the exact optimal policy with efficient computation and data use.

The result depends on several explicit assumptions. Hidden-state transitions must be deterministic. Features of hidden states and observations must be connected through a conditional Hilbert space embedding of the observation process. The optimal hidden-state action-value function must be linear in the state features, and its action values must have a gap. Together, these conditions provide the structure used by the algorithm.

The computational and statistical costs grow polynomially with the planning horizon and the intrinsic dimension of the observation features, without explicit dependence on the sizes of the underlying spaces. The authors also show that deterministic transitions and the action gap are necessary to avoid exponential statistical complexity in the horizon or dimension within their setting. The contribution therefore combines an efficiency guarantee with an explanation of why its structural assumptions matter.
icml-2023-computationally-efficient-pac-.tldr: Under explicit embedding, determinism, linearity, and action-gap assumptions, the paper gives an efficient algorithm for exact optimal control in large POMDPs.

paragraphs: Learning causal relationships often requires interventions: deliberately changing variables and observing what happens. Because interventions can be expensive or risky, choosing informative experiments matters. This paper studies Bayesian experimental design when several experiments must be selected together, including experiments that intervene on multiple variables at once.

Existing approaches described by the authors assemble batches greedily and use black-box optimization to choose an individual intervention target and value. The proposed method instead makes the design process differentiable and optimizes a batch through gradients. A parameterization of the design space allows the procedure to jointly search over which variables to intervene on and which values to assign them.

This joint formulation makes a complicated experimental design problem accessible to a single end-to-end optimization procedure. Across synthetic datasets, the authors report better performance than the evaluated baselines and acquisition strategies in both single-target and multiple-target settings. The findings support gradient-based batch design as a useful approach to selecting causal experiments, with the reported empirical evidence specifically coming from synthetic data.
icml-2023-differentiable-multi-target-ca.tldr: The paper jointly optimizes batches of causal interventions through gradients and reports improvements over existing strategies on synthetic datasets.

paragraphs: A pretrained encoder can provide useful representations for new tasks, but adapting a large network can overwrite knowledge from earlier tasks. This paper introduces a discrete key-value bottleneck to make adaptation more localized when training data changes over time, particularly in continual learning.

The architecture first encodes an input, then uses that representation to select nearby keys from a collection of learnable key-value pairs. The corresponding values are passed to a decoder that solves the task. Only a sparse selection of pairs is accessed for any input. This creates a way to make updates depend on the current context rather than involving every stored pair.

The authors theoretically examine how the bottleneck can limit the effects of learning under distribution shifts and show that it reduces hypothesis-class complexity. In class-incremental experiments, the method reduces catastrophic forgetting across a variety of pretrained models and outperforms relevant baselines. These results are obtained without supplying task boundaries, supporting the architecture’s usefulness when the learner is not explicitly told where one task ends and another begins.
icml-2023-discrete-key-value-bottleneck-.tldr: A sparse, discrete key-value layer enables localized adaptation and reduces forgetting in evaluated continual-learning settings without task boundaries.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks a classifier to work on a new distribution without seeing target-domain data during training. When training examples come from several source domains, a few domains or classes can dominate the learning process. This paper proposes Distribution Free Domain Generalization, or DFDG, to counter that imbalance through standardization.

The method expresses discrepancies across domains and classes using pairwise two-sample test statistics. These statistics provide a way to compare distributions within the training data. DFDG then balances their importance or covariance structures so that a dominant domain or class does not disproportionately determine the training objective. The key idea is therefore to change how cross-domain differences are measured and weighted.

The authors establish a generalization bound for multiclass classification and report superior performance in empirical studies. They also emphasize that the procedure uses fewer hyperparameters, making implementation and tuning easier and faster. The theoretical and empirical contributions address complementary questions: how the procedure’s generalization can be analyzed, and whether its balancing strategy helps on the evaluated prediction problems.
icml-2023-distribution-free-domain-gener.tldr: DFDG standardizes pairwise domain and class discrepancies to reduce dominance during training and improve generalization to unseen domains.

paragraphs: Label shift occurs when class frequencies change between training and testing while the distribution of features within each class stays the same. This paper develops ELSA to estimate adaptation weights for that setting. Its motivation is that existing approaches can have substantial estimation error or require additional calibration after prediction.

The authors first derive a moment-matching framework using the geometry of influence functions. In practical terms, the framework turns information from the two distributions into equations for the adaptation weights. ELSA solves linear systems to obtain those weights, providing a computationally direct procedure without a separate post-prediction calibration step.

The estimator has two stated asymptotic properties: its error shrinks at the square-root rate in the source sample size, and its scaled error approaches a normal distribution. Experiments show that ELSA can achieve state-of-the-art estimation performance while avoiding the calibration overhead. These results concern the specified label-shift setting; the unchanged feature distribution within each class is central to the problem the method addresses.
icml-2023-elsa-efficient-label-shift-ada.tldr: ELSA estimates label-shift adaptation weights through linear systems, with asymptotic guarantees and strong empirical performance without post-prediction calibration.

paragraphs: Training a deep network becomes difficult when its gradients shrink toward zero or grow excessively. This paper studies that problem for maxout networks by analyzing gradients with respect to both inputs and model parameters. The goal is to derive initialization choices from the network’s gradient behavior rather than treating initialization as an isolated tuning decision.

The authors bound gradient moments in terms of the architecture and the distribution of parameters. They find that the distribution of the input-output Jacobian depends on the input, adding a complication to stable initialization. Using their moment analysis, they formulate initialization strategies that avoid vanishing and exploding gradients in wide networks.

Experiments with deep fully connected and convolutional maxout networks show improvements in training with both SGD and Adam. The paper also develops refined bounds on the expected number of linear regions, analyzes expected distortion of curve lengths, and gives results concerning the neural tangent kernel. Together, these contributions connect practical initialization to a broader mathematical account of how maxout networks transform inputs and propagate gradients.
icml-2023-expected-gradients-of-maxout-n.tldr: Gradient-moment analysis yields initialization strategies that stabilize wide maxout networks and improve evaluated SGD and Adam training.

paragraphs: Kernel principal component analysis can be costly to train because its usual computation involves a singular value decomposition of the Gram matrix. This paper revisits the optimization underlying kernel PCA to obtain faster algorithms and make the method easier to extend with different objectives.

The authors use dualization of an objective expressed as a difference of convex functions. This reformulation leads to gradient-based algorithms that avoid the expensive matrix decomposition. It also creates a common route for modifying the objective rather than developing an unrelated procedure for each extension. In particular, the paper studies objectives expressible as Moreau envelopes to promote robustness and sparsity within the same framework.

Evaluations on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show significant training-time speedups and illustrate benefits in robustness and sparsity. The contribution is therefore both computational and methodological: the reformulation changes how kernel PCA is solved and broadens the objectives it can accommodate. The reported experiments support these advantages for the tested benchmarks without requiring a separate framework for each desired property.
icml-2023-extending-kernel-pca-through-d.tldr: A dual optimization formulation enables faster gradient-based kernel PCA and extensions that promote robustness and sparsity.

paragraphs: An agent with little or no reward feedback still needs a principled way to explore an unknown environment. This paper studies two entropy objectives: encouraging diverse visitation and encouraging diverse complete trajectories. Distinguishing these objectives matters because their statistical costs can have different dependence on the desired accuracy.

For visitation entropy, the authors first propose a game-theoretic algorithm whose sample complexity scales as H³S²A/ε², up to logarithmic factors. Here H is episode length, S and A count states and actions, and ε is the target error. For trajectory entropy, they exploit its connection to entropy-regularized decision processes to obtain a bound polynomial in S, A, and H, with inverse-linear dependence on ε.

The authors then apply regularization techniques to visitation entropy, improving its bound to H²SA/ε² up to logarithmic factors. They interpret the trajectory result as establishing a potential statistical advantage of regularization for exploration. The improved visitation result also establishes a statistical separation between maximizing exploration entropy and reward-free exploration, showing that these exploration goals need not demand the same amount of data.
icml-2023-fast-rates-for-maximum-entropy.tldr: New entropy-exploration algorithms improve sample-complexity guarantees and establish potential statistical benefits from regularization.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning seeks efficient ways to remove the influence of data from a learning procedure. This paper approaches the problem by representing learning algorithms as sequences of adaptive queries from structured classes. It develops efficient unlearning algorithms for linear and prefix-sum queries, then uses reductions to apply them to broader learning problems.

For stochastic convex optimization, the guarantees expose a tradeoff controlled by a positive parameter ρ. Unlearning uses roughly ρ times the gradient-query cost of retraining, up to logarithmic factors. For smooth Lipschitz losses, the excess population-risk bound combines a 1/√n term with √d/(nρ), where n is the original sample size and d is model dimension. For nonsmooth losses, the second contribution becomes the square root of that ratio.

For generalized linear models, including linear and logistic regression, the paper obtains dimension-independent rates, with different exponents for smooth and nonsmooth losses. It also extends the framework beyond one deletion request to streams containing insertions and deletions. The contribution is a reusable query-based route to unlearning guarantees that explicitly relate computational savings to statistical accuracy.
icml-2023-from-adaptive-query-release-to.tldr: A structured adaptive-query framework yields efficient unlearning algorithms with explicit computation–accuracy tradeoffs and extensions to dynamic data streams.

paragraphs: This paper develops an autoencoder that treats both the latent variables associated with individual examples and the decoder’s shared parameters probabilistically. The aim is to support flexible prior distributions and posterior approximations while keeping inference costs low. This extends Bayesian treatment across both local representations and global model parameters.

The inference method uses amortized Markov chain Monte Carlo: an implicit stochastic network learns to generate samples from the posterior over local latent variables. The authors then place a sparse Gaussian process prior over the latent space. They also treat its inducing points and kernel hyperparameters in a fully Bayesian way, and report that this extension improves scalability.

The framework additionally accommodates deep Gaussian process priors and missing data. Experiments examine dynamic representation learning and generative modeling, with strong reported performance against existing methods combining Gaussian processes and autoencoders. The contribution brings together flexible latent structure and learned posterior sampling, while extending probabilistic treatment to quantities that govern the Gaussian process itself.
icml-2023-fully-bayesian-autoencoders-wi.tldr: A fully Bayesian autoencoder combines learned posterior sampling with sparse Gaussian process latent priors for scalable representation learning and generation.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can struggle to discover useful behavior from scratch, even when demonstrations, offline data, or an existing policy are available. Simply using that information to initialize learning can work poorly, particularly for value-based methods. Jump-Start Reinforcement Learning offers a different way to organize the help provided by prior behavior.

The algorithm maintains a guide policy and an exploration policy. The guide creates a curriculum of starting states from which the exploration policy learns. This makes existing behavior useful through the states it provides for further learning. The authors present JSRL as a meta-algorithm compatible with any reinforcement-learning approach and able to incorporate the stated forms of prior information.

On simulated robotic tasks, JSRL significantly outperforms the evaluated imitation-learning and reinforcement-learning methods, especially when data is limited. The paper also provides a sample-complexity upper bound. Its theory shows that help from a guide can change the horizon dependence of non-optimistic exploration methods from exponential to polynomial, giving a formal account of how guided starting states can ease exploration.
icml-2023-jump-start-reinforcement-learn.tldr: JSRL uses a guide policy to create starting-state curricula, improving exploration empirically and yielding stronger sample-complexity guarantees.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples to label, often favoring examples near a decision boundary. The usual hope is better prediction from the same labeling budget, despite additional computation. This paper investigates why margin-based selection can instead perform worse than passive learning when the data has many dimensions.

For logistic regression, the authors prove a high-dimensional setting in which passive learning outperforms margin-based active learning. The result persists even with noiseless data and sampling based on the Bayes-optimal decision boundary. Those conditions matter because they show that neither label noise nor an inaccurate sampling boundary is needed for the demonstrated failure.

The proof points to a mechanism distinct from explanations developed for low-dimensional problems. It also suggests that weaker separation between classes makes the phenomenon worse. Experiments on 20 high-dimensional datasets across several application areas corroborate that intuition. The result challenges a blanket preference for margin-based sampling: sophisticated example selection can lose its expected advantage under the high-dimensional conditions studied, even when the boundary information used for sampling is ideal.
icml-2023-margin-based-sampling-in-high-.tldr: In the high-dimensional logistic-regression setting studied, passive learning can beat margin-based active learning even with noiseless labels and an optimal sampling boundary.

paragraphs: Transformers can be difficult to train on small datasets, making pretrained models attractive starting points. This paper examines pretrained attention weights, especially in vision models, to identify structural patterns that might help explain the advantage. It then turns those observations into a simple initialization scheme.

The scheme sets the product of the query and key weight matrices approximately equal to the identity matrix. It sets the product of the value and projection matrices approximately equal to the negative identity. These relationships imitate patterns found in pretrained Transformers, giving the method its name, mimetic initialization. The construction is closed form and requires no learning to produce the initialization.

The authors report faster training and higher final accuracy for vanilla Transformers, particularly on vision classification tasks. Reported accuracy gains exceed 5% on CIFAR-10 and 4% on ImageNet. The finding shows that these simple relationships among attention weights can provide a useful starting structure. In the evaluated settings, some training benefits associated with the observed pretrained weight patterns can therefore be obtained through initialization alone.
icml-2023-mimetic-initialization-of-self.tldr: A learning-free initialization that imitates pretrained attention-weight patterns improves Transformer training speed and final accuracy in evaluated vision tasks.

paragraphs: Gaussian mixture copula models offer greater expressiveness than Gaussian mixture models, but estimating their parameters presents difficult obstacles. Their likelihood lacks a closed-form expression, complicating both expectation-maximization and direct likelihood optimization. This paper addresses that computational obstacle together with a separate problem: different parameter choices can be non-identifiable.

The authors prove the source of non-identifiability and propose suitable priors that eliminate it. They also develop an efficient numerical framework for evaluating the otherwise intractable likelihood and provide analytical derivatives. These contributions address two different needs in estimation: making the objective computable and resolving ambiguity in its parameterization.

The paper further describes the model as a sequence of invertible transformations starting from a base distribution. This viewpoint opens a route to expressing Gaussian mixture copula models in modern probabilistic programming languages. Empirical evidence from synthetic and real-world datasets supports the main claims. Together, the results aim to make a flexible model more practical by improving its estimation foundations and its compatibility with probabilistic modeling tools.
icml-2023-on-the-estimation-of-gaussian-.tldr: The paper addresses Gaussian mixture copula estimation through identifiability-resolving priors, numerical likelihood evaluation, and analytical derivatives.

paragraphs: Deep networks can favor simple but weakly predictive features while overlooking more informative features that are harder to compute. Spurious correlations in incomplete training data can worsen this simplicity bias. This paper proposes a feature sieve that intervenes in the network to reduce reliance on such easy shortcuts.

The method aims to identify and suppress easily computed spurious features in lower layers. That suppression is intended to let higher layers extract and use richer representations. A central feature of the approach is that it does not require supplied knowledge of which attributes are biased or spurious, reducing dependence on manually specifying the shortcuts to avoid.

Experiments on controlled datasets and real-world images provide evidence of both suppression and enhancement of relevant features. The authors report substantial gains on multiple debiasing benchmarks, including an 11.4% relative gain on ImageNet-A. They also outperform many baselines that receive information about known biased attributes. These findings support intervening on feature learning itself as a practical way to counter simplicity bias in the evaluated settings.
icml-2023-overcoming-simplicity-bias-in-.tldr: The feature sieve suppresses easy spurious features without predefined bias attributes and improves performance on evaluated debiasing benchmarks.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning tries to improve prediction by learning related tasks together. Sharing information can also backfire when one task harms another, a failure known as negative transfer. This paper develops a computationally efficient multi-task extension of supervised learning methods based on principal component analysis and analyzes when that sharing helps or hurts.

The analysis shows that the default learning procedure can suffer dramatic failure through negative transfer. It also identifies simple adjustments to data labels that prevent this problem and necessarily improve performance within the analyzed framework. The label treatment is therefore a substantive part of the method: the theoretical benefit comes from correcting how the tasks enter the learning procedure.

Experiments on synthetic and real-data benchmarks show performance comparable to state-of-the-art multi-task methods at substantially lower computational cost. The contribution pairs an efficient learning construction with an explanation of a central failure mode. It also provides a theoretically supported correction, giving the empirical efficiency results a connection to how information is shared across tasks.
icml-2023-pca-based-multi-task-learning-.tldr: A PCA-based multi-task method uses theoretically motivated label adjustments to avert negative transfer while achieving competitive performance at lower computational cost.

paragraphs: After a classifier reaches zero training error, further training often makes examples from the same class have increasingly similar internal features. Class means also approach a structured geometric arrangement. Idealized models can predict exact neural collapse, but practical networks commonly stop short because later layers cannot freely reshape all earlier features.

This paper introduces a model that requires optimized features to remain near a predefined feature matrix, such as intermediate network features. The authors study small neighborhoods through perturbation analysis. This constraint represents limited freedom to change the input features and allows the model to describe departures from exact collapse.

The analysis proves a reduction in within-class variability relative to the predefined features by studying gradient flow along a central path with minimal assumptions. It also characterizes minimizers near collapse and examines how regularization settings influence proximity to collapse. Experiments in practical deep-learning settings support the theory. The contribution explains aspects of partial collapse that unconstrained feature models, whose minimizers collapse exactly, cannot capture.
icml-2023-perturbation-analysis-of-neura.tldr: Constraining features to stay near an initial representation enables a perturbation analysis of incomplete neural collapse and regularization effects.

paragraphs: Training on a smaller dataset is useful only if the selected examples retain the information needed for learning. This paper constructs coresets for radial basis function neural networks: small weighted subsets designed to approximate the full dataset’s loss across networks in the relevant class. The authors present this as the first such construction for these networks.

The work draws on their ability, with enough hidden units, to approximate continuous functions on closed bounded sets to arbitrary precision. It specifically develops coresets for radial basis and Laplacian loss functions. The authors then use the construction to obtain a provable data-subset selection procedure for training deep neural networks.

The connection to training is that the gradient of each network weight is itself a function of the input. The paper uses its function-approximation framework to justify approximating those gradients with the weighted subset. Empirical evaluations cover function approximation and dataset selection across popular architectures and datasets, demonstrating the construction’s efficacy and accuracy. This connects subset selection to preserving training-relevant functions rather than merely reducing the number of examples.
icml-2023-provable-data-subset-selection.tldr: The paper constructs weighted coresets for radial basis function networks and uses them to derive provable subset selection for neural-network training.

paragraphs: Some prediction problems call for understanding one particular variable rather than explaining every input equally. A treatment variable or a sensitive attribute may deserve focused scrutiny. PWSHAP addresses this need by explaining the targeted effect of a binary variable in a complex outcome model through distinct pathways.

The framework combines the predictor with a user-defined directed acyclic graph. It uses this graph together with on-manifold Shapley values to identify effects along causal pathways while maintaining robustness to adversarial attacks. The graph supplies the pathway structure, making it an explicit component of the explanation rather than something supplied by the predictive model alone.

The authors establish error bounds for both Shapley values and the path-wise effects. They show that the method supports local bias and mediation analyses that remain faithful to the model. When the targeted variable is randomized, it can additionally quantify local effect modification. Examples and a real-world experiment demonstrate the explanations’ resolution, interpretability, and locality, emphasizing what happens for particular cases rather than only providing aggregate summaries.
icml-2023-pwshap-a-path-wise-explanation.tldr: PWSHAP combines a user-defined causal graph with Shapley values to explain a binary variable’s local effects along distinct pathways.

paragraphs: A prediction can be explained by identifying which training examples contribute to it. This paper develops such explanations for regularized high-dimensional models, assigning importance weights to individual training samples. The resulting high-dimensional representers connect a model’s output to the data used to fit it.

The central result is a representer theorem that decomposes a prediction into contributions from training samples. A positive contribution supports the prediction in the positive direction, while a negative contribution acts in the opposite direction. The authors derive specific consequences for sparse models using ℓ1 regularization and low-rank models using nuclear-norm regularization, extending the explanation framework across these two important model structures.

The paper further develops the low-rank case for collaborative filtering and instantiates representers for popular model classes in that setting. Empirical studies cover three real-world binary-classification datasets and two recommender-system datasets. Demonstrations of recommendation explanations show how the decomposition can make a model output understandable through relevant training examples and their signed contributions.
icml-2023-representer-point-selection-fo.tldr: A new representer theorem explains regularized high-dimensional predictions as signed contributions from individual training examples.

paragraphs: Weak supervision replaces some manual annotation with simple labeling rules, but making those rules reliable can still require extensive expertise and validation. This paper introduces WS-VAE to reduce sensitivity to how carefully labeling functions are engineered. It combines weak labels with unsupervised learning of the input representation.

The model learns jointly from inputs and their weak labels, using a latent space to capture the input distribution. Its representation-learning component regularizes the inference of weak labels. A specially designed decoder also learns how relevant each labeling function is for each input, allowing the model to account for relevance at the example level.

These components let information in the inputs help interpret the weak supervision signals. On a standard weak-supervision benchmark, the authors report performance competitive with state-of-the-art methods and substantially greater robustness to labeling-function engineering. The main finding is that jointly modeling inputs and weak labels can reduce dependence on carefully constructed rules, while preserving competitive predictive performance in the evaluated setting.
icml-2023-robust-weak-supervision-with-v.tldr: WS-VAE jointly learns input representations and weak labels to reduce sensitivity to labeling-rule quality while maintaining competitive performance.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes are often viewed as less capable of representation learning than neural networks. One approach to narrowing that gap uses inter-domain variational Gaussian processes whose inducing variables correspond to neural-network hidden units. This paper examines practical issues with that approach and develops a more flexible approximation.

The proposed extension uses an orthogonal decomposition of the Gaussian process into principal and orthogonal components. Spherical inter-domain features provide data-dependent basis functions for both components. This gives the approximation flexibility in how it represents the data across the two parts, while retaining the connection to neural-network activation features.

The authors show that incorporating those activation features in the proposed framework alleviates the practical shortcomings they study and scales better than alternative strategies. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness. The contribution is a way to organize neural-style features within a Gaussian process approximation so that representation flexibility and computational scalability can be addressed together through the same construction.
icml-2023-spherical-inducing-features-fo.tldr: Spherical features in an orthogonally decomposed Gaussian process improve representation flexibility and scalability in the proposed approximation framework.

paragraphs: Many optimization problems ask which subset of available items should be selected under constraints. This paper introduces a class of set functions that supports efficient approximation algorithms through a restricted form of submodularity. The restriction is defined relative to an ordering of the items, called a submodular order.

The functions must also be monotone and subadditive: adding items does not reduce value, and combining sets does not exceed the sum of their separate values. The additional order-based condition supplies enough structure for fast maximization algorithms with strong approximation guarantees under several constraints. The contribution identifies useful algorithmic structure in this limited form of submodularity.

The authors apply the framework to constrained assortment optimization in fundamental choice models, obtaining faster algorithms and stronger guarantees. For some cases, these are the first constant-factor approximation guarantees. They also connect the framework to streaming maximization of monotone submodular functions, recovering the best known approximation guarantees as a consequence. This links assortment selection and streaming optimization through the same order-based mathematical property.
icml-2023-submodular-order-functions-and.tldr: A restricted, order-based form of submodularity yields fast approximation algorithms for assortment selection and recovers strong streaming guarantees.

paragraphs: Adapting a model to a new domain is especially difficult when only one target example is available. Standard data augmentations may provide too little variation to address a large distribution shift. This paper proposes SiSTA, which uses that single example to guide a generative model toward the target domain.

SiSTA first fine-tunes a generative model from the source domain using the target example. It then uses new sampling strategies to curate synthetic target data. The central idea is to make the generated training variation responsive to the observed target, giving adaptation a source of examples shaped by the new domain despite the very limited target data.

Experiments span multiple benchmarks, distribution shifts, and image corruptions in face-attribute detection and multiclass object recognition. The authors report significantly better generalization than existing baselines and competitive performance against models trained with larger target datasets. These results support target-aware generation as a useful augmentation strategy in the tested single-shot settings, where adapting the source generator provides more effective data for adaptation.
icml-2023-target-aware-generative-augmen.tldr: SiSTA adapts a source generative model using one target example and samples synthetic target data to improve single-shot domain adaptation.
